[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Stashing Changes in Git: A Comprehensive Guide"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Git stash is a powerful feature that allows you to temporarily shelve changes you've made in your working directory so you can work on something else, and then come back and re-apply them later. This is particularly useful when you need to switch branches quickly to fix a bug or address an urgent issue without committing half-finished work."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Basic Usage: Stashing and Re-applying"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"The most basic use case involves stashing your current changes and then re-applying them. Here's how:"},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"# Stash your current changes
git stash"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"This command saves your uncommitted changes (both staged and unstaged) to a stash. Your working directory will then revert to the state of your last commit."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"# List your stashes
git stash list"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"This command shows a list of all your stashes. Each stash is identified by an index (e.g., stash@{0}, stash@{1})."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"# Re-apply the most recent stash
git stash apply"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"This command applies the most recent stash (stash@{0}) to your working directory. The stash remains in the stash list."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"# Re-apply a specific stash
git stash apply stash@{2}"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"This command applies the stash at index 2 to your working directory. The stash remains in the stash list."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"# Remove the most recent stash after applying
git stash pop"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"This command applies the most recent stash (stash@{0}) and then removes it from the stash list. It's equivalent to 'git stash apply' followed by 'git stash drop'."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"# Remove a specific stash
git stash drop stash@{1}"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"This command removes the stash at index 1 from the stash list."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"# Clear all stashes
git stash clear"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"This command removes all stashes from the stash list. Use with caution!"},{"order":19,"type":"subheading","text":"Stashing Untracked Files"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"By default, 'git stash' only stashes tracked files (i.e., files that Git is already aware of). To also stash untracked files, use the '-u' or '--include-untracked' option:"},{"order":21,"type":"code","text":"# Stash tracked and untracked files
git stash -u"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"To stash all files, including ignored files, use the '-a' or '--all' option:"},{"order":23,"type":"code","text":"# Stash all files (tracked, untracked, and ignored)
git stash -a"},{"order":24,"type":"subheading","text":"Creating a Stash with a Message"},{"order":25,"type":"paragraph","text":"It's helpful to add a message to your stashes to remember what they contain. Use the '-m' or '--message' option:"},{"order":26,"type":"code","text":"# Stash with a message
git stash save -m "Fixed a bug in the login form""},{"order":27,"type":"subheading","text":"Stashing Specific Files"},{"order":28,"type":"paragraph","text":"While 'git stash' typically stashes all changes, you can stage specific files and then stash only the staged changes:"},{"order":29,"type":"code","text":"# Stage specific files
git add file1.txt file2.txt

# Stash only the staged changes
git stash push -m "Stashed changes to file1 and file2""},{"order":30,"type":"subheading","text":"Creating a Branch from a Stash"},{"order":31,"type":"paragraph","text":"If the changes in your stash are significant enough to warrant their own branch, you can create a new branch from a stash:"},{"order":32,"type":"code","text":"# Create a new branch from a stash
git stash branch <branchname> stash@{0}"},{"order":33,"type":"paragraph","text":"This command creates a new branch named <branchname>, checks out that branch, and applies the stash at stash@{0}. The stash is then dropped from the stash list."},{"order":34,"type":"subheading","text":"Resolving Conflicts After Applying a Stash"},{"order":35,"type":"paragraph","text":"When you apply a stash, conflicts may arise if the code in your working directory has changed since the stash was created. You'll need to resolve these conflicts manually, just like with a merge or rebase. After resolving the conflicts, stage the changes and commit."},{"order":36,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices"},{"order":37,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always add a message to your stashes to make it easier to identify them later."},{"order":38,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use 'git stash list' frequently to keep track of your stashes."},{"order":39,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Consider creating a branch from a stash if the changes are substantial and warrant their own development effort."},{"order":40,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Be mindful of untracked and ignored files when stashing. Use the appropriate options ('-u' or '-a') if needed."},{"order":41,"type":"paragraph","text":"By following these guidelines, you can effectively use 'git stash' to manage your changes and streamline your Git workflow."}]
